title: good company
hook: an old chain of verses that starts with who you sit with and ends in freedom

segments.voice: Yesterday, moksha, and a boy who told Death to keep his gold. Your line was freedom is the point. Did you set something down, even for a breath? One more word before the camp ends. Day twenty.

Yesterday's word was the top of the mountain: freedom. Fair question, then. Where do you start? There's an old Sanskrit song called Bhaja Govindam, traditionally credited to the teacher Shankara, and one of its verses answers that question like a row of dominoes. Each step knocks over the next, all the way up to freedom. You'd expect the first domino to be something hard. Years of study. Fasting. A cave in the mountains. It isn't. The very first domino is who you spend your time with.
screen: `WHERE DO YOU START?` → `A ROW OF DOMINOES.` → `THE FIRST ONE: YOUR COMPANY.`

segments.voice: Satsang. Sat means true, real, good. Sang means company, being together. Satsang is good company, the company of what's true and of people turned toward it. Here's the chain from Bhaja Govindam, in plain words. From good company comes letting go. From letting go comes freedom from delusion. From freedom from delusion comes a mind that stays steady. And from a steady mind comes freedom while you're still alive. Look at what's in that chain. Delusion: think of the snake on the rope from day eighteen. Freedom is moksha from yesterday. And the thing that starts it all isn't a technique. It's a room. In Hindu life, a satsang is often an actual gathering. People meet in a home or a temple hall to sing, to hear a teacher, to read a text together, to sit in silence side by side. Nobody has to be advanced. You come, you sit, you listen. The idea underneath the verse is simple and a little uncomfortable: company shapes a person. A friend's worries can become your worries; a grandmother's patience can become your patience. The verse doesn't say go find perfect people. It puts company first in the chain, and leaves the question with you: what is your company doing to you, and how much time do you spend near what's true? That first domino has a name and a face.
screen: `SAT — TRUE. SANG — COMPANY.` · `GOOD COMPANY, THEN LETTING GO, THEN FREEDOM.` · `A ROOM, NOT A TECHNIQUE.` · `WE TAKE THE SHAPE OF OUR COMPANY.` · then, large: `GOOD COMPANY CHANGES YOU.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: sit in company. Sit and breathe. Bring to mind one person whose presence makes you steadier. A friend, a grandparent, a teacher, someone in a story. Let their face come. Notice what happens to your breathing near them. Then widen it, to anyone, anywhere, who stops today to pray or to sit still. Let yourself be one of them. If you pray, you can hold them all before God. The bell holds the time.
Satsang. Good company. The company of what's true, and the first domino on the way to freedom. Twentieth word.
Your line: good company changes you. Today, spend ten unhurried minutes with one person who steadies you. In person, if you can. Day twenty.

howItsDone: Hindus gather for satsang in homes, temples and ashrams to sing bhajans, hear a teacher, read scripture together and sit in silence, and some families hold one on special days.

fork.setup: you want the steadiness this path keeps pointing toward. the old verse gives you a row of dominoes. which one do you push first?
options: a long retreat alone in the mountains.
fork.reveal: Bhaja Govindam starts with satsang: from good company comes letting go, and the chain runs all the way to freedom while living.

original.note: Sanskrit: sat, true or good, and sanga, company. The company of what's true.

trapdoor: what you thought: satsang is a meeting with a guru.
what it means: good company, the company of what's true and of people turned toward it. it can be any room.
what a scholar hears: Bhaja Govindam's verse running from satsangatva to jivanmukti, freedom while living, traditionally credited to Shankara.

sources.ref: Bhaja Govindam (Moha Mudgara), verse 9, traditionally attributed to Adi Shankara

notes: Bhaja Govindam verse (satsangatve nissangatvam, nissangatve nirmohatvam, nirmohatve nishchalatattvam, nishchalatattve jivanmuktih) paraphrased; usually numbered verse 9, numbering varies by edition. Attribution to Shankara given as 'traditionally credited'. Confirm.
'Nirmohatvam' rendered as 'freedom from delusion' and linked back to day 18 (maya); 'nishchalatattvam' as 'a mind that stays steady'. Confirm these glosses.
Sat and sanga glossed as parts of the compound (true/good + company); this is a meaning gloss, not a historical etymology. Confirm.
'We take on the shape of the people we keep close' is the script's own observation, not attributed to a text; manuscript's 'one of the oldest observations' cut.
Original: सत्सङ्ग (also written सत्संग), pronounced SUT-sung; confirm.

Editor pass: cut 'this path has had a quiet satsang running under it… other people sitting at sunset with the same bell… you haven't been doing this alone' and the practice's 'others on this path… some at it for years' (unproven claims about other users, plus a stock line); teach now ends on the first domino having a name and a face. 'The tradition doesn't say' made 'the verse doesn't say'; 'delusion is the snake' softened to 'think of the snake'; howItsDone 'families often' made 'some families'.

Audit (2026-10-01): Bhaja Govindam chain and glosses checked; no factual errors. 'People take on the shape of those they keep close' was stated as fact by the narrator; now framed as the idea underneath the verse ('company shapes a person', with 'can become'). Cut the closing repeat of 'isn't a technique' (already said two sentences earlier). Note 'nirmohatvam' is freedom from moha (delusion, infatuation), not maya; the link to day 18 is only 'think of', which seems fair.
